name: Ginpu (吟風, Hokkaido sake rice)
text: Hokkaido's first sake rice with a shinpaku (white core) and, per prefectural sources, the most widely brewed of the three Hokkaido sake rices today. Bred at the Hokkaido Central Agricultural Experiment Station from a 1990 cross, [(Hattanishiki No.2 x Joiku 404) F1] x Kirara397, line name Kuiku 158, and adopted as a Hokkaido recommended variety in March 2000. A second source gives the cross in a different parent order, so quote the pedigree from the station's original report.
flavor: Rounded, full and tending sweet; the richer end of the Hokkaido trio.
use: Junmai to ginjo class sake from Hokkaido breweries such as Otokoyama and Kamikawa Taisetsu; also bought by breweries outside Hokkaido.
craft: The station report names weak cold tolerance and large year-to-year yield variation as its flaws, which is why Kitashizuku was bred afterwards. Because shinpaku expression is good, the grain dissolves readily; check each harvest's protein and water uptake before fixing polishing ratio and steaming. Expect a fuller, sweeter result than Suisei at the same polishing.
src: HRO: Breeding of the new sake rice Ginpu
J-STAGE: Hokkaido sake rices Ginpu, Suisei, Kitashizuku

name: Suisei (彗星, Hokkaido sake rice)
text: Hokkaido-bred sake rice with low protein content, a heavy thousand-grain weight (large grains) and high yield. In brewing comparisons it sits at the clean, dry (tanrei) end of the Hokkaido trio, opposite the richer Ginpu. The search results gave no breeding year or cross for Suisei, so none is stated here.
flavor: Light, clean, dry-leaning, with few off-notes.
use: Tanrei karakuchi junmai and ginjo from Hokkaido breweries; frequently put side by side with Ginpu in tasting flights.
craft: Low protein supports high polishing and a clean finish, but it also means a lighter body, so a brewer who wants weight adjusts koji ratio and fermentation rather than expecting it from the rice. Large heavy grains need uniform soaking, timed by stopwatch rather than by feel. Read the cultivar on the label when comparing against Ginpu or Kitashizuku.
src: Hokkaido Rice Sales Expansion Committee: Suisei
J-STAGE: Hokkaido sake rices Ginpu, Suisei, Kitashizuku

name: Kitashizuku (きたしずく, Hokkaido sake rice)
text: Hokkaido sake rice released in 2014 (Heisei 26), bred after Ginpu's weak cold tolerance and yearly variability became a problem. The HRO breeding report lists high cold tolerance among its traits. Brewers place it between Ginpu (dissolves readily, gives flavour) and Suisei (clean and dry), and one brewer calls it the best of both.
flavor: Between Ginpu's fullness and Suisei's cleanness; balanced and moderately round.
use: Junmai and ginjo for Hokkaido breweries, e.g. Otokoyama's Kitashizuku junmai.
craft: Choose it when you want Ginpu-like flavour with Suisei-like finish and a more reliable harvest. As a newer cultivar its brewing data are still accumulating, so keep batch records per rice lot and polishing ratio.
src: HRO: Breeding of the new sake rice Kitashizuku (PDF)

name: Otokoyama and Asahikawa soft water (男山と旭川の水)
ja: 男山と旭川の仕込み水
text: Otokoyama of Asahikawa presents its sake as brewed with Daisetsuzan permanent-snow subsoil water, drawn from a spring in front of the main brewery and from a well; its style is described as tanrei karakuchi. The city of Asahikawa reports tap-water hardness of about 20 to 40 mg/L (Ishikari River plant 23.0, Chubetsu River plant 40.3), i.e. soft; below 120 mg/L is generally counted as soft. One article notes a Tokachi brewery using medium-hard water, so Hokkaido water is not uniform.
flavor: Clean, light and dry; soft water gives an unobtrusive profile.
use: Reference case for Hokkaido soft-water, tanrei karakuchi sake.
craft: Hardness figures here are municipal tap water, not the brewery's own well, so ask the brewery for its own analysis. Soft water ferments more gently and tends toward a delicate result; adjust koji and temperature management rather than assuming style.
src: Jizake Kuramotokai: Otokoyama water, rice, skill

name: Hanafubuki (華吹雪, Aomori junmai sake rice)
text: Large-grained Aomori sake rice bred at the Aomori Agricultural Experiment Station and used mainly for junmai sake, described as giving a rich yet clean taste. Its shinpaku tends to sit off-centre, so it does not suit very high polishing. Sources disagree on the date: one says it was bred in 1985, another that use began in 1986. It was later the pollen parent of Hanaomoi.
flavor: Koku (body) with a clean, crisp finish.
use: Junmai and tokubetsu junmai from Aomori breweries; blended with Hanaomoi in some top bottlings.
craft: Keep polishing in junmai range and use Hanaomoi when you need 40% polishing. Off-centre shinpaku raises the risk of cracking if over-milled, so check the broken-grain rate after each polishing run.

name: Hanaomoi (華想い, Aomori daiginjo sake rice)
text: Aomori sake rice for ginjo and daiginjo. The registration record states it was bred in 1987 at the Aomori Agricultural Experiment Station by crossing Yamadanishiki with Aomori-kei Sake 97 (later named Hanafubuki), and registered on 9 March 2006 (No. 13863); the name dates from about 2002. Small dot- or line-shaped shinpaku and low protein allow 40% polishing, comparable to Yamadanishiki. Wikipedia says Hanafubuki was the pollen parent and Yamadanishiki the seed parent, the aim being to bring in Hanafubuki's lodging resistance.
flavor: Clean, umami-rich and crisp, with a distinct shinpaku-derived body.
use: Junmai daiginjo from Aomori breweries, e.g. Denshu Junmai Daiginjo 140 (Hanaomoi, Yamadanishiki, Hanafubuki).
craft: Use Hanaomoi when you need a local rice for 40% polishing, which Hanafubuki cannot take. Treat steaming and koji-making as you would for Yamadanishiki but test each lot's water absorption.

name: Ginebōshi and Hana-sayaka (吟烏帽子・華さやか, newer Aomori sake rices)
text: Two newer Aomori sake rices. Ginebōshi was designated a prefectural variety in 2018 (Heisei 30); it tolerates cold, can be grown in cool districts, and gives a showy aroma with a clean taste. Hana-sayaka is described as lower in amino acid content than Hanafubuki and Hanaomoi, bred with sake-style diversity in mind. The results did not include their breeding records.
flavor: Ginebōshi: fragrant and clean. Hana-sayaka: light, low amino-acid character.
use: Prefectural brand sake for brewers wanting a lighter or more aromatic Aomori style.
craft: Low amino acids in Hana-sayaka point to a cleaner, drier finish and less need to manage umami and acid. Both are recent, so request the prefecture's brewing data and run trial lots before committing a whole season.
src: Sake Times: Aomori sake rice tasting

name: Mahoroba Hana yeast (まほろば華酵母, Aomori)
text: A yeast developed jointly by an Aomori research institution and the Brewing Society of Japan. Aomori sources describe the Mahoroba yeasts as aromatic and as a deciding factor in the character of Aomori sake. The results gave no strain number, development date or fermentation data, so only its role is recorded.
flavor: Aromatic, fruity ginjo character.
use: Aomori ginjo and junmai ginjo, often paired with prefectural rices such as Hanaomoi.
craft: Ask the individual brewery or the Aomori technology institute for the exact strain and temperature recommendation, since the sources give no process numbers.
src: Sake Times: Aomori sake rice tasting

name: Tsugaru Toji (津軽杜氏, Aomori brewing masters)
text: The toji of the Tsugaru region, mostly from Hirosaki, who with the Nambu toji supported Aomori's local sake. The Tsugaru Toji Association no longer exists because breweries decreased, and few toji trained in it remain. One explanatory article, written about ten years before it was read, said there were about ten such toji in the 1980s and about five then; the figure is undated, so treat it as approximate.
flavor: A farming-and-brewing tradition rather than a flavour style.
use: Context when reading Aomori bottlings or visiting Hirosaki-area breweries.
craft: Historically a toji farmed in summer and brewed in winter, a pattern that is fading. As union training lapsed, newer toji come from owner-brewers and other routes, so ask each brewery who the toji is and where they trained.
src: Sake and Utensil Science: three great toji groups

name: Nambu Toji (南部杜氏, Iwate master brewers' guild)
text: One of Japan's three great toji groups, originating in Shiwa, Iwate and based in Ishidoriya, Hanamaki. Narrative sources trace its start to around 1600, when Nambu domain merchants brought Itami's large-batch cask method. The guild began with 220 members, rose to 500 and then 1,000 within a few years of the Taisho era (the source's Western dates are inconsistent), peaked at 4,153 in 1965, and stood at 554 members including 175 toji in May 2026. It became the Nambu Toji Association in 1948 and an incorporated association in 1953.
flavor: Associated with soft, clean, rice-driven sake from low-temperature, long fermentation.
use: Check the guild affiliation of the toji when selecting Tohoku sake; influential in Miyagi as well.
craft: The association runs training and a toji qualification exam. A brewery blog lists requirements as full membership, age 27 or over, a completed special course, and experience as kashira, koji-maker or moto-maker; this is not an official statement. About 300 people gather for the July seminar.
src: Serai: Iwate sake and Nambu toji

name: GI Iwate (地理的表示「岩手」)
text: National Tax Agency geographical indication for Iwate sake, designated 25 September 2023. The production standard defines it as sake with a soft mouthfeel and rice-derived rich umami, supported by Iwate's famous waters and Nambu toji skill, stressing mineral-rich subsoil water and a cold climate suited to low-temperature fermentation. A news report says a stricter tier, 'GI All Iwate', additionally requires Iwate-grown rice.
flavor: Soft entry with rice-derived richness; styles range from rich-sweet to clean.
use: Look for the GI mark when sourcing sake guaranteed to be brewed in Iwate to the standard.
craft: The GI guarantees the production standard, while the All Iwate tier tightens rice origin; read the exact label wording, since the two are different claims. Check the full standard on the NTA page for water and rice conditions.
src: NTA: list of GI for alcohol

name: Ginginga and Ginotome (吟ぎんが・ぎんおとめ, Iwate sake rices)
ja: 吟ぎんが・ぎんおとめ
text: Iwate Agricultural Research Center sake rices. Ginginga is a mid-season variety with strong cold tolerance and good brewing suitability, a standard Iwate sake rice. Ginotome is an early variety suited to central and northern Iwate. Both were aimed at ginjo sake at around 50% polishing, which is why brewers later asked for a daiginjo rice and Yui no Ka was bred.
flavor: Clean, soft Iwate profile; ginjo-friendly.
use: Junmai and ginjo from Iwate breweries; the prefecture's staple sake rices.
craft: Both are designed for roughly 50% polishing, so move to Yui no Ka or Yamadanishiki for daiginjo. One summary gave parentage inconsistently, so it is omitted here.
src: Iwate Sake Brewers Association: Iwate sake rice
Iwate Prefecture: Yui no Ka breeding report (PDF)

name: Yui no Ka (結の香, Iwate daiginjo sake rice)
text: Iwate daiginjo rice, a cross of Yamadanishiki with Aomori-kei Sake 140, selected over ten years and numbered Iwate Sake 98. Developed by the Iwate Industrial Technology Center with the brewers' association, farmers and the agricultural research center, aiming to rival Yamadanishiki when brewers wanted a daiginjo rice beyond the 50% grade of Ginginga and Ginotome. It has a shorter culm than Ginginga and gives clear sake with little off-flavour.
flavor: Clear and clean, with few off-notes.
use: Iwate junmai daiginjo and daiginjo, marketed as Iwate's top rice.
craft: Shorter culm than Ginginga helps against lodging in the field; in the brewery treat it as a high-polish rice and check lot protein. Confirm the label states Iwate-grown Yui no Ka.
src: Iwate Prefecture: Yui no Ka breeding report (PDF)
Iwate Sake Brewers Association: sake rice

name: Reimei Heisen koji (黎明平泉, Iwate original koji mold)
text: An Iwate-original koji mold described by the Iwate Sake Brewers Association as made by combining two original koji molds and suited to Iwate rice. It is the koji counterpart to the prefecture's sake rices. The results did not give strain parents or the year of release.
flavor: Intended to complement Iwate rices; style not described in the source.
use: Used by Iwate breweries as a prefectural identity marker alongside local rice and water.
craft: Ask whether Reimei Heisen is used for all koji or only part of the batch; the brewers' association page is the reference for the current official description.
src: Iwate Sake Brewers Association: Iwate yeast and koji

name: Miyagi Junmai-shu no Ken declaration (みやぎ・純米酒の県)
ja: みやぎ・純米酒の県宣言
text: In November 1986 the Miyagi Sake Brewers Association declared Miyagi a 'junmai-shu prefecture', and all 52 member companies began brewing junmai from 100% Sasanishiki, a table rice known for its taste. It is reported as the only such prefecture-wide declaration. The share of tokutei meisho-shu is quoted as 92%, 94% or 96% depending on the source.
flavor: Clean, light, dry (tanrei karakuchi), the typical Miyagi profile.
use: Explains why Miyagi shops and menus lean toward junmai; Ichinokura's Sasanishiki junmai daiginjo is an example.
craft: When quoting tokutei meisho percentages, cite source and year because the figures differ. Sasanishiki is a table rice, so ask a brewery how it handles it for sake and what polishing it uses.
src: Miyagi Shunsen Tanbo: why Miyagi sake is good

name: Kura no Hana (蔵の華, Miyagi sake rice)
text: Miyagi's first prefectural sake rice, registered as a recommended variety in 1997. It is large-grained and absorbs water well, has low acidity and amino acids and low protein, and tolerates cold and lodging. Many Miyagi breweries use it, and it gives light, crisp sake. It is also one of the two parents of Yamagata's Yukimegami.
flavor: Light, crisp and clean.
use: Miyagi junmai and ginjo; basis of the tanrei karakuchi Miyagi style.
craft: Good water absorption and easy dissolving mean you manage soaking and koji ratio to avoid over-melting. Low amino acids give a clean finish, so body must come from process if wanted.
src: Miyagi Shunsen Tanbo: why Miyagi sake is good

name: Ginno Iroha (吟のいろは, Miyagi sake rice)
text: Newer Miyagi-bred sake rice that appeared in 2020, the first new prefectural sake rice since Kura no Hana. The name was chosen by a naming committee centred on the Furukawa Agricultural Experiment Station. It is easier to grow than Kura no Hana and is described as giving rounder, softer, fuller sake.
flavor: Soft, rounded and full-bodied.
use: Miyagi junmai ginjo and similar; positioned as the successor to Kura no Hana.
craft: Its selling point is cultivation ease plus a softer, fuller result than Kura no Hana; compare lots side by side when choosing a rice for a house style.
src: Miyagi Shunsen Tanbo: why Miyagi sake is good

name: Miyagi tanrei karakuchi and Nambu-toji tradition (宮城の淡麗辛口)
ja: 宮城の淡麗辛口と南部杜氏
text: Miyagi sake is generally described as tanrei karakuchi (light, dry), attributed to the low-temperature, long fermentation of the Nambu toji, who spread brewing culture in the early Edo period and remain the mainstream. Serai traces Miyagi brewing to patronage by the Sendai domain lords.
flavor: Light, dry and crisp; made for food.
use: Food-pairing sake in Sendai, consistent with the prefecture's junmai focus.
craft: To reproduce the style, control the moromi temperature curve for a long, low fermentation and avoid over-extracting amino acids. The sources give no figures.
src: Miyagi Shunsen Tanbo: why Miyagi sake is good
Serai: Miyagi junmai sake and Sendai domain

name: Akita Sake Komachi (秋田酒こまち)
text: Akita's prefectural sake rice, bred in 2001 at the Akita Agricultural Experiment Station by crossing Akikei Sake 251 and Akikei Sake 306, and made a recommended variety in 2003. Large-grained with a small shinpaku, it takes high polishing and suits ginjo and daiginjo. Descriptions give rice umami, elegant sweetness and rich aroma.
flavor: Rice umami with refined sweetness and a rich aroma.
use: Akita ginjo and daiginjo; also junmai at lower polishing, e.g. Mansaku no Hana Akita Sake Komachi 70.
craft: The small shinpaku allows high polishing without much cracking. As a recent cultivar, ask each brewery for polishing ratio and check lot protein before ginjo-grade batches.
src: Hinomaru Jozo: Mansaku no Hana Akita Sake Komachi 70

name: AK-1 Akita Ryuka-bana yeast (秋田流花酵母)
text: Akita's own ginjo yeast, born in 1990 (Heisei 2) from joint research between the prefecture and the Akita Sake Brewers Cooperative that began in 1987, ahead of the nationwide ginjo boom. It corresponds to Kyokai yeast No. 1501. It gives refreshing, light sake with moderate ginjo aroma and a light aftertaste.
flavor: Refreshing, light, moderate ginjo aroma, light finish.
use: Akita ginjo and junmai ginjo.
craft: A moderate-aroma yeast, so keep fermentation cool and long in the Akita style to preserve the light finish. Do not confuse with Kyokai No. 6, which the cooperative site credits to the Shinsei (Aramasa) brewery.
src: Akita Sake Brewers Cooperative: yeast story (2)
Government of Japan Online: Akita sake

name: Akita-style cold-season brewing (秋田流寒造り, low-temperature long fermentation)
ja: 秋田流寒造り(低温長期醗酵)
text: The Akita Sake Brewers Cooperative presents Akita-style kanzukuri (low-temperature, long fermentation) as the basis of its ginjo brewing. Winter snow stabilises brewery temperature so the moromi ferments slowly at low temperature. Koji is made in a room kept at 25-35 C for about two days even in midwinter. The cooperative says good brew water has moderate minerals and little iron and manganese. One brewery describes a season starting in November and peaking from December to February.
flavor: Smooth, clean and light, as the cooperative describes the result.
use: Reference process for understanding Akita ginjo and why the region favours long cold fermentation.
craft: Key checks: koji room temperature through the cold season, brew water iron and manganese, and a moromi temperature curve that stays low for a long time. Ratios and exact temperatures were not given in the sources.
src: Akita Sake Brewers Cooperative: secrets of Akita sake
Akita Sake Brewers Cooperative: brewing process

name: Sannai Toji (山内杜氏, Akita master brewers)
text: Toji from the Sannai district of Yokote, Akita. The association was founded in 1922 as the Sannai Toji Training Association, resumed in 1949 as the Sannai Village Toji Association after wartime suspension, and took its present name in 1959. Its aims were training toji, improving technique and supplying brewery workers. In 2022 it marked 100 years with 145 members, and its annual summer seminar reached its 95th run.
flavor: A guild tradition tied to Akita's cold-season style.
use: Context for Akita breweries, many of which now use a local or owner toji.
craft: The seminar is held in Yokote before the Obon holiday. Association coverage says the traditional group form has declined in favour of owner-toji, local hires and young and female toji, so check each brewery's current toji.
src: Akita Sake Brewers Cooperative: Akita toji

name: Dewa Sansan (出羽燦々, Yamagata sake rice)
text: Yamagata's first original sake rice, from Misayama-nishiki x Hanafubuki, and the most grown in the prefecture, mainly for ginjo. Its shinpaku is of medium size and protein slightly low. The birth year differs by source: 1994 (JA), 1995, or 1985 (theDANN), so quote the year with its source. Line name Yamagata Sake 49.
flavor: Fragrant and soft.
use: Ginjo and junmai ginjo; the required rice for DEWA33 certification.
craft: Medium shinpaku and low protein give soft, aromatic sake that works well with Yamagata yeast. Track grain size and polishing break rate by lot.

name: Yukimegami (雪女神, Yamagata daiginjo rice)
text: Yamagata's first daiginjo-class rice, line Yamagata Sake 104, from Dewa no Sato x Kura no Hana. A newspaper reports development began in FY2010 with full use from 2017, while Wikipedia says it began in 2001. Thousand-grain weight about 26.9 g, roughly 1 g above Dewa Sansan, with higher shinpaku expression and lower protein. Dewazakura sells a 48% polished version.
flavor: Clean, with little off-flavour.
use: Junmai daiginjo and daiginjo; the basis of the Yamagata Sanka brand.
craft: Small point-shaped shinpaku allows polishing above 50% without cracking; Yamagata's YK009 yeast was designed for it. Confirm development years with Yamagata's technology centre because sources disagree.
src: Kahoku: Yamagata first in national new sake
Yamagata Sake Brewers: DEWA33, Sanka, Dewa no Sato, Yukimegami

name: Dewa no Sato (出羽の里, Yamagata junmai rice)
text: Yamagata rice developed as the successor to Dewa Sansan for junmai sake. It has large grains, a shinpaku that tends to sit at the centre, and low protein. It is also one of the two parents of Yukimegami.
flavor: Soft, clean junmai character.
use: Yamagata junmai and junmai ginjo.
craft: A central shinpaku is more forgiving than an off-centre one; test its water absorption separately from Dewa Sansan, since grain size differs.
src: Yamagata Sake Brewers: DEWA33, Sanka, Dewa no Sato, Yukimegami

name: DEWA33 (Yamagata junmai ginjo standard)
text: A Yamagata Sake Brewers Association certification: 100% Dewa Sansan, junmai ginjo, polishing 55% or less, Yamagata yeast and the original Oryze Yamagata koji mold. Passing the tasting panel earns the DEWA33 title and a certificate. The name comes from the 33 peaks over 1,400 m in the prefecture and from Dewa Sansan. Many bottles are polished to 50%.
flavor: Fruity, soft junmai ginjo.
use: Look for DEWA33 on the label as a brewery's local-resource junmai ginjo.
craft: Sake Street adds in-prefecture brew water as a condition, but the association page does not state it. Polishing of 55% is an upper limit, so 50% bottles exceed the requirement.
src: Yamagata Sake Brewers: DEWA33, Sanka, Dewa no Sato, Yukimegami

name: Yamagata Sanka (山形讃香)
text: A prestige junmai daiginjo brand developed by Yamagata Prefecture and the Yamagata Sake Brewers Association, aiming at the highest peak of Japanese sake. The raw rice is gold-medal entry rice from a Yukimegami competition. The polishing ratio was not confirmed in the results.
flavor: Top-grade clean junmai daiginjo.
use: Top-class Yamagata bottle for gifting and competitions.
craft: The brand ties rice quality to contest-winning lots; verify the current standard on the association page before quoting figures.
src: Yamagata Sake Brewers: DEWA33, Sanka, Dewa no Sato, Yukimegami

name: Yamagata KA and YK009 yeasts (山形KA酵母・YK009)
text: The Yamagata Prefecture Industrial Technology Center developed a high-aroma yeast by selecting cerulenin-resistant strains from a distributed parent strain, producing Yamagata KA yeast. A brewery source says KA gives pear and banana-like aroma and a later Yamagata yeast (2008) gives ripe apple. YK009 is a newer strain made for Yukimegami, balancing ethyl caproate (apple) and isoamyl acetate (banana) at low acidity.
flavor: KA: pear and banana aroma, refined. YK009: balanced apple and banana, low acidity.
use: Yamagata ginjo and daiginjo; YK009 for Yukimegami.
craft: Names overlap (Yamagata yeast, KA, NF-KA, YK009), so ask which strain a brewery used. The sources give no fermentation temperatures.
src: Yamagata Industrial Technology Center: high-aroma yeast (PDF)

name: GI Yamagata (地理的表示「山形」)
text: Geographical indication for Yamagata sake, designated 16 December 2016. The production standard requires domestic rice and rice koji, water taken within Yamagata, no sugar additions, and brewing, storage and bottling within the prefecture.
flavor: Not a flavour standard; a regional origin guarantee.
use: Check the label for GI Yamagata; it signals in-prefecture brewing and water.
craft: The standard covers materials and location, not style. Read the full text on the NTA page before making label claims.
src: NTA: list of GI for alcohol

name: Yume no Ka (夢の香, Fukushima sake rice)
text: Fukushima's original sake rice bred at the Fukushima agricultural centre and registered in 2003. Parents are Hattanishiki No.1 and Yamagata Sake 49 (Dewa Sansan). It was bred to replace Gohyakumangoku, is somewhat more cold and lodging tolerant, and has a large but crack-resistant shinpaku, suiting ginjo and daiginjo. Another source says crossing began in 2000.
flavor: Fragrant, clean ginjo character.
use: Fukushima ginjo, e.g. Aizu Chujo Junmai Ginjo Yume no Ka and Kokken.
craft: Low breakage in polishing allows high polishing. It is paired with Utsukushima Yume yeast in the Fukushima brand scheme.
src: Fukushima Sake Brewers: brand sake Yume no Ka

name: Fukunoka (福乃香, Fukushima sake rice)
text: Second Fukushima original sake rice, added in 2019. One parent is Homarefuji, which came from Yamadanishiki irradiated with gamma rays, so the rice carries Yamadanishiki blood from both sides. Retail pages pair it with Yume no Ka, as in Tenmei's Fukunoka x Yume no Ka bottling.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: Fukushima junmai ginjo and similar premium bottlings.
craft: The sources give no brewing data, so ask the brewery for polishing ratio and tasting notes. The word 'hybrid' used by a shop was not confirmed in the results.
src: Jizake.com: Tenmei Fukunoka x Yume no Ka
Fukushima original sake rice project team

name: Utsukushima Yume yeast and Fukushima Brand Sake (うつくしま夢酵母)
ja: うつくしま夢酵母・ブランド酒
text: The Fukushima Sake Brewers Cooperative's 'dream rice, dream sake' brand: sake made with Yume no Ka rice and Utsukushima Yume yeast, produced only inside the prefecture. One page spells the yeast differently (Utsukushima Kira yeast), and the cooperative's name is written shuzo kyodo kumiai on its site.
flavor: Fragrant ginjo style.
use: Look for the brand mark on Fukushima bottles.
craft: The brand pairs a local rice with a local yeast; ask the brewery about koji and polishing, which the sources do not specify.
src: Fukushima Sake Brewers: brand sake Yume no Ka
Tsurunoe Shuzo: Aizu Chujo Yume no Ka

name: Aizu Toji (会津杜氏)
text: Aizu toji association founded in 1989 (Heisei 1) to train brewing skill and successors. Aizu once invited Echigo and Nambu toji for the brewing season; now owner-toji and local toji lead many breweries. The association says Aizu brewers contributed to Fukushima leading gold-award counts, and members include a Modern Master Craftsman awardee and a Medal with Yellow Ribbon recipient.
flavor: A guild tradition rather than a flavour style.
use: Context for Aizu breweries.
craft: A column credits Aizu-Wakamatsu brewing's early development to the Aizu domain's protection in the Edo period.

name: Fukushima gold-award record and Sake Academy
ja: 福島の全国新酒鑑評会金賞と清酒アカデミー
text: At the 114th National New Sake Appraisal (announced May 2026) Fukushima took 20 gold medals, the most of any prefecture, for the second year running; Niigata and Nagano followed with 16 and Hyogo had 14. The local paper counts it as Fukushima's 13th top finish and says it held nine in a row to 2022. Training centres on the Fukushima Sake Academy, a vocational school run by the prefectural brewers' association. A mission document puts Fukushima fourth nationally in brewery count, with over 60 in Hamadori, Nakadori and Aizu (undated).
flavor: Gold-award sake is a ginjo style prepared for the contest.
use: A signal of ginjo technique concentration in Fukushima.
craft: Contest sake is a special ginjo and does not equal the daily product; judge in the cup.
src: Fukushima Minyu: second year number one

name: Hitachi Nishiki (ひたち錦, Ibaraki sake rice)
text: Ibaraki's first original sake rice. Breeding started in 1991 and it was registered as a variety in 2003. Low protein reduces off-flavour and suits a clean style.
flavor: Clean, light.
use: Ibaraki junmai and junmai ginjo, e.g. Aoki Shuzo's Gokeiji, which uses Hitachi Nishiki and a prefectural yeast.
craft: Low protein gives a clean base; adjust koji and acid if more body is wanted.

name: Pure Ibaraki (ピュア茨城)
text: Ibaraki Sake Brewers Association's all-Ibaraki junmai project, started in 2003 (Heisei 15). The association lists four rices: Hitachi Nishiki, Fukumaru, Ichibanboshi and Yumehitachi. Brewery pages describe Hitachi Nishiki 100% with Ibaraki's own 'Hitachi yeast' and 32 participating breweries under one specification. Polishing of 55% is common but is a per-brewery spec rather than a confirmed common rule.
flavor: Rice-forward junmai that shows brewery character.
use: Standard-grade local junmai; look for Pure Ibaraki on the label.
craft: Rice lists differ by source; read the label for the rice and yeast actually used.

name: Hitachi Toji (常陸杜氏)
text: Ibaraki's toji certification, launched in 2019 by the Ibaraki Sake Brewers Association with the prefectural industrial innovation centre, to train local toji and brand Ibaraki sake; three people were certified first. The exam is held about once a year. A sake-information article lists the requirements as 3 or more years as production manager (7 or more in the production site otherwise), completion of the prefecture's sake college toji course, first-class sake brewing technician or intent to obtain it, 40 points in the brewer career register, and an employer's recommendation.
flavor: Not a flavour style.
use: Context when assessing Ibaraki breweries that no longer depend on outside toji.
craft: The requirements come from a private article from around 2020, so confirm current rules with the association.

name: Shimotsuke Toji (下野杜氏, Tochigi)
text: Tochigi's prefecture-wide toji qualification, created by the Tochigi Sake Brewers Association in FY2006 with the Tochigi Industrial Technology Center, which sets the curriculum and exams (practical, sensory and written). Nikkei calls it a 21st-century toji group. One article says the system joined the national toji federation in 2012; that date is unconfirmed. Unlike migrant toji, they are in the brewery year-round.
flavor: Not a flavour style.
use: The association holds an annual Shimotsuke Toji new sake showing, with a 2026 Osaka event reporting 18 breweries.
craft: Year-round employment changes the staffing model compared with seasonal migrant guilds; ask who holds the toji role in a brewery.
src: Tochigi Sake Brewers: What is Shimotsuke Toji
Sake Times: Shimotsuke Toji new sake 2026

name: Tochigi prefectural yeasts (T-1, T-Delta)
text: By 1993 four Tochigi original yeasts existed, including T-Delta and T-1, which have gold-award records. They were developed by Okamoto Takemi of the Tochigi Industrial Technology Center, who visited about 40 breweries, collected some 2,000 to 3,000 house-yeast samples and selected through repeated brewing trials over about two years. Sources do not give strain characteristics.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: Tochigi-only profile for breweries wanting a locally derived yeast.
craft: The strains came from brewery-resident yeast selection, so each strain's behaviour should be requested from the technology centre.

name: Yume Sasara (夢ささら, Tochigi sake rice)
text: Tochigi's sake rice from Yamadanishiki (mother) x T-Sake 25 (disease-resistant father), started in 2005 and taking 13 years under the working name Tochigi Sake 27. Registered February 2018. It matures earlier and resists lodging better than Yamadanishiki, has a shinpaku as large as or larger than Yamadanishiki, and is higher in crude protein, potassium and umami amino acids. In 2019, 27 Tochigi breweries brewed it simultaneously.
flavor: Umami and sweetness from amino acids.
use: Daiginjo and junmai ginjo from Tochigi breweries.
craft: Higher protein and amino acid content than Yamadanishiki means more body; adjust polishing and fermentation for the style wanted. It does not crack easily when polished.

name: Maikaze and Gunma KAZE yeast (舞風・群馬KAZE酵母)
text: Maikaze is a Gunma-bred sake rice registered with MAFF in March 2011. The 'all-Gunma' Maikaze brand, developed with the Gunma Sake Brewers Association, the Agricultural Technology Center and the Industrial Technology Center, requires 100% Maikaze, a Gunma yeast such as Gunma KAZE yeast or Gunma G2 yeast, Gunma water and junmai. Product labels cite Gunma KAZE yeast No. 2.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: All-Gunma junmai, junmai ginjo and daiginjo.
craft: The yeast's development year and aroma profile were not in the results; check the strain designation on the label.

name: Wakamizu (若水)
text: Sake rice bred in Aichi in 1983 from Aichi-kei Sake 101 (seed parent) and Gohyakumangoku (pollen parent). It resists lodging and cold but is weak to disease and is grown from Ibaraki, Tochigi and Gunma to Oita. A page says Gunma Wakamizu was the first Kanto rice certified as sake rice. Wakamizu is also the father of Saitama's Sake Musashi.
flavor: Rice umami, deep and concentrated.
use: Kanto prefectural sake in Ibaraki, Tochigi, Gunma, Kanagawa and elsewhere.
craft: Disease susceptibility makes crop quality year-dependent, so judge each harvest. Aichi sources give the pedigree; check against the registration record.

name: Sake Musashi (さけ武蔵, Saitama sake rice)
text: Saitama sake rice developed in 2004 by the prefecture's agriculture research centre from Kairyo Hattanryu (mother) and Wakamizu (father), over 12 years. Large grain and large shinpaku, but soft, so unsuitable for high polishing; it dissolves and breaks easily and is awkward to handle. It yields a rounded, clean sake. 17 Saitama breweries use it, and Kagamiyama won a gold award with it.
flavor: Rounded, clean, with good swell of flavour.
use: Saitama junmai and ginjo, including Kagamiyama's Sake Musashi bottlings.
craft: Because it is soft and dissolves readily, consider short soaking and a restrained koji and steaming approach. The prefecture's technology centre ran analysis and brewing trials to document its handling.
src: Saitama Industrial Technology Center: Sake Musashi

name: Saitama yeast and Saitama G yeast (埼玉酵母・埼玉G酵母)
text: The Saitama Industrial Technology Center North Institute in Kumagaya has developed, managed and distributed Saitama yeast since the 1960s, mainly to prefectural breweries. Saitama G yeast, a ginjo yeast developed jointly with RIKEN, is described as giving a gorgeous aroma and umami. One brewery uses Saitama G for ginjo-type sake.
flavor: Gorgeous aroma with umami.
use: Saitama ginjo and junmai ginjo.
craft: Distribution is to Saitama sake producers, so a bottle naming Saitama G signals a prefectural-resource product; check the technology centre for strain details.

name: Chichibu sake and Mt. Bukou water (秩父の酒)
ja: 秩父の酒と武甲山伏流水
text: Chichibu has three to four breweries depending on the source. Bukou Shuzo (Bukou Masamune, founded 1753, Horeki 3) uses Mt. Bukou subsoil water, selected as one of Heisei's 100 famous waters; Yao Honten (Chichibu Nishiki) dates from 1749 (Kanen 2); Taisei's Chichibu Kojiro is a third label. Sources disagree on the water: one calls it soft, another says it is rare medium-hard water rich in minerals because it passes through a limestone mountain.
flavor: Not described reliably in the sources.
use: Chichibu brewery visits and local pairing.
craft: Because softness is disputed, request the brewery's own hardness figure rather than relying on an article.

name: Fusa no Mai (総の舞, Chiba sake rice)
text: Chiba's own sake rice, from Shiratae-nishiki (mother, sake rice) and Chubu 72 (father, table rice), created because Chiba had relied on outside rice for ginjo. It is a mid-season rice resistant to lodging, cold damage and blast, and is grown only in Chiba; output was recorded as 83 t in 2015. Dates differ: development from 1993, variety registration in 2000 per one source, or 2001 breeding / Heisei 12 per others.
flavor: Not described in detail in the sources.
use: Takeoka Tokubetsu Junmai (Wakura Shuzo), Kidoizumi's Junmai Nama AFS from Isumi-grown Fusa no Mai, and a 55% Katori junmai ginjo.
craft: Chiba's association defines ginjo as 60% or less and daiginjo 50% or less. Koizumi Shuzo grows it itself from 2024 with Kanozan-system water.

name: Kidoizumi high-temperature yamahai and AFS (木戸泉)
text: Kidoizumi Shuzo of Chiba (Isumi) developed a high-temperature yamahai moto, adopted from 1956 (Showa 31) under its third head. One source puts the moto temperature at 55 C, explained as saccharifying starch while heat-sterilising; another says it removes unwanted microbes. AFS is a thick, high-acid sake pressed from a single-stage mash with lactic acid use. In 1965 the brewery succeeded in sake able to age long term and began making aged sake; it holds 5, 10 and 40+ year stocks.
flavor: Thick, high acid, lactic and aged character.
use: Aged sake and acid-forward bottlings, e.g. AFS Old Reserve.
craft: The unusual part is a hot moto, a single-stage mash, and long ageing; these defy standard three-stage practice. Details like ratios should come from the brewery.

name: Ozawa Shuzo and the two waters of Ome (小澤酒造・澤乃井)
ja: 小澤酒造と澤乃井の二つの水
text: Ozawa Shuzo (Sawanoi, Sawai, Ome) was founded in 1702 (Genroku 15). It uses two waters: a cave spring from a lateral well hand-dug about 140 m into Chichibu Paleozoic rock behind the brewery, medium-hard and mineral-rich, said to give vigorous fermentation and a firm, crisp sake; and a soft mountain well water from roughly 4 km away (other pages say several km) across the Tama River. Using both lets the brewery range from dry to sweet, and sources say the soft water is used for kimoto.
flavor: Medium-hard water: firm, crisp. Soft water: gentle.
use: A reference case for blending waters of different hardness in one brewery.
craft: No hardness values in mg/L were given, so obtain the brewery's analysis. Choosing the water per brew is a deliberate quality tool.
src: and trip: two springs of Ozawa Shuzo

name: Tama sake of Tokyo (東京多摩の酒)
text: The Tokyo Sake Brewers Association lists one brewery in the 23 wards and nine in Tama; one article counts only nine in all, and the list also shows Tsuchiya Shuzo as suspended. Ozawa Shuzo (Sawanoi, Ome) was founded in 1702, Ishikawa Shuzo (Tamajiman, Fussa) began making sake in 1863, and Toshimaya Shuzo (Higashimurayama) makes Okunokami. Tama is described as having soft water from the Chichibu mountain system.
flavor: Delicate, soft-water profile as described by regional guides.
use: Tama brewery visits and urban-edge pairing.
craft: Counts vary by source and date, so check the association list before quoting a number.

name: Tokyo Port Brewery and Edo Kaijo (東京港醸造)
ja: 東京港醸造・江戸開城
text: The only brewery in the 23 wards, in a four-storey building in Shiba, Minato. Toji Terasawa Yoshimi, with over 40 years' experience, developed the compact 'craft kura' brewing equipment. It began with doburoku in 2011 and received a seishu licence in September 2016; its main label is Edo Kaijo. A Nikkei headline says it brews with Minato ward tap water. Yeast origin differs by source: dancyu says a home-cultured No. 9-type yeast; another article credits an original 'Tokyo yeast' developed with a vocational school in Ota ward.
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: A case study in small-footprint urban brewing.
craft: One blog notes that yeasts named Tokyo or Edo in the Kyokai lineage were named in 1908 and may not be Tokyo-derived, so do not assume origin from the name.
src: Hands On Local: Tokyo Port Brewery
Nikkei: Edo Kaijo from Minato tap water

name: Tanzawa-water sake of Kanagawa (丹沢の水と神奈川の酒)
ja: 神奈川の酒と丹沢伏流水
text: Many Kanagawa breweries use Tanzawa subsoil water, giving a clear, transparent taste. Brewery count is 14 on the prefecture page, 13 on the association page, and 12 to 15 elsewhere. The association says junmai share is high among mostly small breweries; a ranking site notes higher average polishing than other prefectures and rices such as Yamadanishiki, Misayama-nishiki and Wakamizu.
flavor: Clear, clean and tending dry.
use: Food-pairing sake; the 12 breweries' autumn festival in Yokohama.
craft: Counts differ by source, so cite the source and date.

name: Izumibashi estate-grown rice (泉橋酒造・いづみ橋)
text: Izumibashi Shuzo of Ebina, founded 1857, polishes all its rice in-house and grows 90% of it locally in Ebina. Its Megumi Blue Label junmai ginjo uses 100% locally grown Yamadanishiki, polished to 58%; the name Megumi is explained as coming from the moral teaching go-on go-kei (五恩五恵).
flavor: Not described in the sources.
use: A model of grower-brewer integration in the Kanto plain.
craft: The key control is in-house polishing combined with local cultivation, which lets the brewer track a lot from field to bottle.

name: S. tokyo yeast of Nakazawa Shuzo (S.tokyo酵母)
text: Saccharomyces tokyo Nakazawa, discovered in 1909 by Dr Nakazawa Ryoji of Tokyo University of Agriculture. Sources disagree on where: Munich brewing institute, or isolated from a moto. Described as the second oldest surviving sake yeast and never used in sake until release. Nakazawa Shuzo's 11th head, Kagiwada Akira, obtained it from the university's culture collection and released Matsumidori Junmai Ginjo S.tokyo in October 2018, fermenting slowly at 14 C because it is unsuited to usual cold fermentation.
flavor: Compared to white wine in a news headline.
use: A heritage-yeast bottling from the Ashigara area.
craft: Fermentation at 14 C rather than the usual low range is the key setting. One interview page spells the discoverer's given name 亮二 where most sources write 亮治.

name: Kan-zake temperature names (燗酒の温度名称)
text: Common warming names: hinata-kan about 30 C, hitohada-kan 35 C, nuru-kan 40 C, jo-kan 45 C, atsu-kan 50 C, tobikiri-kan 55 C or higher. These are informal rather than an industry standard; sources vary on hitohada (35 to 37 C) and jo-kan (45 to 50 C).
flavor: Rises from rice aroma and umami to a sharper, drier edge as temperature goes up.
use: Used when ordering and serving kan-zake.
craft: Touch test: a tokkuri base that feels slightly hot to the finger is about 45 to 50 C.
